passages.t: ‘We do not lose heart’, and light in our hearts
passages.happening:
Paul has described the glory of the new covenant. Now he says what it means for him. “Therefore, since God in His mercy has given us this ministry, we do not lose heart” (verse 1).

He has nothing to hide. “We do not practice deceit, nor do we distort the word of God” (verse 2). He tells the truth openly, before God and before every conscience.

But some do not see it. “And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing” (verse 3). The reason: “The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers so they cannot see the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God” (verse 4).

Paul is not the point of his own message. “For we do not proclaim ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake” (verse 5).

And then Paul reaches back to the first day of creation. “For God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ made His light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
‘Lose heart’ means to grow weary, give up, quit. Paul says it twice in this chapter, at the start and near the end (verse 16). He does not say he never feels like giving up. He says that God's mercy keeps him from doing it.

Verse 2 answers Paul's critics. Some in Corinth seem to have said that he used tricks or twisted his message. Paul says he hides nothing.

The veil of chapter 3 comes back here. If some do not see the light of the gospel, it is not because the light is dim. Something has blinded them. ‘The god of this age’ is a startling phrase. Most readers take it to mean Satan, the enemy of God, who has power in the present world for a time. Jesus spoke of him as “the prince of this world” (John 12:31). ‘This age’ means the present world as it now is, in rebellion against God, before God puts all things right.

‘Jesus Christ as Lord’ may be one of the very first Christian confessions. In Corinth there were many ‘lords’: the emperor, the gods of the temples, masters of slaves. To call Jesus Lord was to say who really rules. And notice how Paul describes himself: your servants. The word can mean slaves.

Verse 6 reaches back to Genesis. The God who spoke light into the darkness at creation has done it again, in human hearts. When Paul met Jesus on the road to Damascus, Acts says a light from heaven flashed around him. Many readers think Paul has that moment in mind here. In ‘the face of Jesus Christ’ people see what God is like.
passages.ot:
Verse 6 echoes the first words God speaks in the Bible: “And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light” (Genesis 1:3). Paul's wording, ‘Let light shine out of darkness’, is not an exact quotation of that verse, but it plainly points to the creation story. Some readers also hear Isaiah: “The people walking in darkness have seen a great light” (Isaiah 9:2).

‘The image of God’ also goes back to Genesis, where people are made “in His own image” (Genesis 1:27). Paul says Christ is the image of God in the fullest sense. Another letter says, “The Son is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15).

The glory in the face of Jesus answers Moses' prayer, “Please show me Your glory” (Exodus 33:18). Moses' face shone after he met God. In Jesus, God's own glory is seen.
passages.asks: Paul says he does not lose heart because of God's mercy, not because of his own strength. Ask what keeps you going when you are tired of doing good. Then ask what you most want people to see when they look at you, and whether it is yourself or Jesus Christ as Lord.

passages.happening:
Paul has spoken of God's glory shining in human hearts. Now he says where that treasure is kept. “Now we have this treasure in jars of clay to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us” (verse 7).

Then come four pairs. “We are hard pressed on all sides, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed” (verses 8-9).

Paul explains what this means. “We always carry around in our body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body” (verse 10). For Jesus' sake they are always being handed over to death, so that his life may be seen in their mortal bodies (verse 11).

And it is for the church's sake. “So then, death is at work in us, but life is at work in you” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Clay jars were the cheapest containers in the ancient world. People kept oil, wine, grain and water in them. They chipped and cracked and were thrown away. No one admired a clay jar. But people did sometimes keep valuable things in plain earthenware, where no one would think to look.

The Corinthians admired impressive people: fine speakers, people of status, people who looked strong. Some looked at Paul and saw a clay jar: an ordinary, worn, battered man. Paul agrees. That is the point. If the messenger is weak, then everyone can see that the power belongs to God.

Look at the four pairs. Each is a real hardship. Each is followed by ‘but not’. Paul does not say ‘we are never pressed’. He says ‘pressed, but not crushed’. The second pair is a play on words in Greek: ‘at a loss, but not utterly at a loss’. The word for ‘despair’ here is the same one Paul used in 1:8, where he admits that he did despair, even of life. So these lines are not a boast that he always feels strong. They are a witness that God held him, even when he could not hold himself.

Verse 10 is bold. Paul's beatings, hunger and danger are a share in what Jesus went through. ‘The death of Jesus’ is carried in his body. But so is ‘the life of Jesus’. The pattern of the cross, death and then life, is being lived out in him. His suffering is not wasted. Through it, life reaches the Corinthians.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament often calls people clay. Isaiah prays, “But now, O LORD, You are our Father; we are the clay, and You are the potter; we are all the work of Your hand” (Isaiah 64:8). God asks Israel, “Just like clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in My hand” (Jeremiah 18:6). Job speaks of “those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundations are in the dust” (Job 4:19).

Valuable things were kept in clay jars. Jeremiah was told to put the deeds of a field he had bought “in a clay jar to preserve them for a long time” (Jeremiah 32:14).

The ‘but not’ of these verses has deep roots in Israel's prayers. “My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalm 73:26). Isaiah says of God's servant, “A bruised reed He will not break and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish” (Isaiah 42:3). And, “He gives power to the faint and increases the strength of the weak” (Isaiah 40:29).
passages.hard:
What if you are not ‘hard pressed but not crushed’? What if you feel crushed?

These verses are not a test you have to pass. Paul is not telling anyone that a true believer never feels crushed or in despair. In this same letter he says plainly that he despaired even of life (1:8). The ‘not crushed’ here is not a feeling Paul produced by trying harder. It is his testimony that God kept hold of him when he could not keep hold of himself.

If you are in a dark place now, you do not have to pretend to be strong, and you do not have to carry it alone. Tell someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor or a counsellor. Paul himself was comforted by a friend's arrival (7:6). If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Seeking help is not a failure of faith. It is one of the ways God sends comfort.
passages.asks: Paul calls himself a clay jar holding a treasure. Ask where your own weakness might be the very place others could see God's power. Then look at the four pairs and ask which one describes a season you have lived through. Who, or what, held you? Who around you is ‘hard pressed’ now, and how could you stand with them?

passages.happening:
Paul quotes a psalm. “And in keeping with what is written: ‘I believed, therefore I have spoken,’ we who have the same spirit of faith also believe and therefore speak” (verse 13).

He keeps speaking because of what he knows. God “who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us with Jesus and present us with you in His presence” (verse 14). It is all for the church's good, so that grace may spread and thanks may overflow to God (verse 15).

Then Paul says again, “Therefore we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day” (verse 16).

“For our light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory that is far beyond comparison” (verse 17).

“So we fix our eyes not on what is seen, but on what is unseen. For what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Paul's hope is not a vague hope. It is the resurrection. God raised Jesus, and he will raise those who belong to Jesus. That is what keeps Paul speaking when speaking costs him so much.

‘Outer self’ and ‘inner self’ may have sounded familiar to Greek hearers. Many Greek thinkers taught that the body is a prison and the soul the real person, who escapes at death. Paul means something different. He has just said that God will raise them, bodies and all (verse 14). The ‘outer self’ is life in this mortal body as it wears down: tired, hurt, growing old. The ‘inner self’ is the new life God is giving, which will be made complete when the body is raised. Paul does not despise the body. He is waiting for its renewal.

Then the words ‘light and momentary’. Remember who is speaking. This is the man who will list his beatings, shipwrecks, hunger and dangers in chapter 11. He was stoned and left for dead. He has just said he despaired of life. When Paul calls his troubles ‘light’, he is not saying they did not hurt. He is weighing them against something else. The Greek word for ‘weight’ is set against ‘light’. In Hebrew, the word for glory comes from a root that means heavy. Paul may be thinking of that: glory is the weightiest thing there is. Next to it, even a life of pain is light, and even a long life is a moment.

‘Fix our eyes’ means to keep looking at something, to aim at it. Faith does not deny what is seen. It keeps looking past it to what God has promised.
passages.ot:
Paul quotes Psalm 116:10. In the BSB, which follows the Hebrew, the line reads, “I believed, therefore I said, ‘I am greatly afflicted.’” (Psalm 116:10). Paul's three Greek words, ‘I believed, therefore I spoke’, follow the old Greek translation of the psalm exactly. The Hebrew is hard to translate, and versions differ. Either way, it is a psalm of a man near death who trusted God and was rescued: “For You have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling” (Psalm 116:8). Paul, who had just been near death himself, speaks with the same faith.

The Psalms also know that life is short. “Let me know how fleeting my life is” (Psalm 39:4). And they know that sorrow does not have the last word: “Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning” (Psalm 30:5).

Isaiah promised renewal to the weary: “But those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength” (Isaiah 40:31).
passages.hard:
‘Our light and momentary affliction.’ This is a much-loved verse, and it can be misused.

Paul says this of his own suffering, with all of chapter 11 behind it. He is not telling anyone else that their pain is light. He weighs his troubles against eternal glory, and from that height they look small. That is his testimony. It is not a line to hand to someone in fresh pain or fresh grief. To a person who has just lost a child, or a marriage, or their health, ‘it is only light and momentary’ is not comfort. It is a wound. Paul himself says in Romans, “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15).

Nor does the verse call suffering good. It says that God is at work even in it, producing something that will far outweigh it. That is a hope to hold, not a reason to stop grieving. As the site's note on Romans 8:28 says, it is never a reason to tell someone who has been hurt that the harm was really good for them.

If your own suffering does not feel light, you are not failing. Many of the psalms are cries of people for whom it did not feel light either. “How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1). God kept those prayers in his book. If it is heavy, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul fixed his eyes on what is unseen. Ask what your eyes have been fixed on lately: what you can see, or what God has promised. Ask where your outer self is wearing down, and whether you see any sign of the inner self being renewed. And when someone near you is suffering, ask whether they need words from you, or simply your company.
